verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED on four independent grounds.

(1) NOTHING IS MISSING. The kind label 'missing-heading' is a misnomer. Both headings are present in the markdown at the correct position, with the clause number and title transcribed verbatim from the PDF: '8.4.2.2 Qualification' (line 6412) and '8.4.2.2.1 General' (line 6415). Both also carry correct hierarchical anchor ids (<a id="section-8-4-2-2">, <a id="section-8-4-2-2-1">). Zero PDF text is lost. The quotations in the claim are accurate; the inference drawn from them is not.

(2) THE PDF CARRIES NO HEADING-LEVEL SIGNAL TO LOSE. I cropped and magnified the printed glyphs at 300 dpi (crop_top.png covering 8.4/8.4.1, crop_bot.png covering 8.4.2.2/8.4.2.2.1). Every heading on page 149 -- 8.4 References, 8.4.1 General, 8.4.2 Uniqueness of reference, 8.4.2.1 General, 8.4.2.2 Qualification, 8.4.2.2.1 General -- is printed in the identical bold serif face, at the identical type size, flush to the identical left margin, with no indentation step and no size step between any of them. ISO conveys clause depth here EXCLUSIVELY through the dotted number, and the markdown reproduces that number exactly. There is no visual distinction in the source for the transcription to have dropped, so there is no PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy to find.

(3) THE CLAIM'S PREMISE IS FALSE: THERE IS NO SCHEME BEING VIOLATED. The claim assumes the transcription maps number-depth to heading-depth and that 8.4.2.2 is an anomalous departure. It does not. Tallying every numbered heading in specs/ISO_COBOL.md: a 4-component number (like 8.4.2.2) is emitted as H2 162 times, H3 620 times, H4 24 times; a 3-component number is H2 276 times, H3 508 times, H4 17 times. The flagged '### 8.4.2.2' is in fact the MAJORITY treatment (620/806 = 77%) for a 4-component number, while the sibling '#### 8.4.2.1' the claim holds up as the correct baseline is the 3% minority outlier. If either heading is the anomaly, it is 8.4.2.1, not 8.4.2.2 -- the claim has it backwards.

(4) THERE IS NO LOCAL OUTLINE TO CORRUPT. The claim's harm story is that clause 8.4.2's outline becomes unwalkable. But the immediate children of 8.4.2.2 already run H3 (8.4.2.2) -> H4 (8.4.2.2.1 General) -> H2 (8.4.2.2.2 General format, line 6442) -> H2 (8.4.2.2.3 Syntax rules). A direct sibling of 8.4.2.2.1 is emitted two levels SHALLOWER than the H2 'References' ancestor three numbering levels above it. The same pattern recurs throughout (8.4.3.1 'Identifier' at H2 under 8.4.3 at H2; 8.4.6.3/.4/.5 at H4 under 8.4.6 at H2). Re-leveling this one heading would not make clause 8.4.2 walkable by a depth-following tool, because the heading levels in this file are undifferentiated noise from the OCR/heading-inference pass rather than an encoding of structure.

CONCLUSION: this is markdown formatting metadata with no counterpart in the source document, it is meaning-preserving, the clause number that actually carries the hierarchy is transcribed correctly, and the specific instance flagged follows the file's dominant convention. It fails the rejection tests for 'text actually present', 'formatting only', and 'does not change meaning'. Not a page-149 discrepancy.

NOTE FOR THE LEDGER (out of scope for this page, offered so it is not lost): the observation that heading depth is unusable for outline-walking across specs/ISO_COBOL.md is TRUE, but it is a single global property of the transcription pipeline affecting ~1,900 headings, not a per-page content discrepancy. Any consumer needing the outline should derive depth from the dotted clause number or the section-N-N-N anchor id, both of which are correct here. If that is worth acting on, it belongs as one global tooling item, not as page-level reconciliation findings.
verdict.corrected_description: No correction to issue -- the finding is rejected outright rather than restated. The heading '8.4.2.2 Qualification' and its child '8.4.2.2.1 General' are both present, correctly numbered, correctly titled, correctly positioned, and correctly anchored; the PDF prints all six page-149 headings at one identical size and margin, so no level information exists in the source to have been lost. The claim's own premise is inverted: H3 is the transcription's majority treatment for a 4-component clause number (620 of 806 occurrences) and the H4 sibling it cites as correct is the 3% outlier.
